EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Common Risk Factors in U.S. Stock and Bond Returns, 1963–1991”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Chosen design: OTHER –  Two-pass (time–series / cross-sectional) factor–pricing framework à la Fama-MacBeth (1973) augmented with a latent-factor sanity check (principal-components‐analysis, PCA).

Why this is appropriate  
•  The question is not “what is the causal impact of a policy shock?” but “which systematic risk factors are priced?”  
•  Asset-pricing theory delivers a well-defined causal model: expected excess return  =  β′λ, where β captures an asset’s causal exposure to the factor(s) and λ is the compensation per unit of exposure. Estimating β from time-series regressions and λ from cross-sectional regressions (or GMM) is the canonical identification strategy.  
•  The time dimension (336 months) provides enough observations to estimate precise betas; the cross-section (hundreds of stocks + bonds) delivers cross-sectional variation to identify factor premia.  
•  PCA is used as a robustness/over-identification check: if the first K principal components line up with the observable factors, our specification is likely correctly specified; if not, unpriced or missing factors are indicated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. “TREATMENT” AND “CONTROL” (interpretation within a factor model)  
Because we are not evaluating a discrete intervention, we reinterpret the requested items:

Treatment variable      Continuous factor exposure β_i,k to factor k (e.g., a stock’s loading on SMB).  
Control group           Assets with β ≈ 0 to that factor serve as the counterfactual.  
Timing / event date     Not applicable; exposures and premia are estimated over the full sample.  
Running variable & cutoff (RDD)     Not applicable.

As an intuitive illustration for readers who like binary comparisons we will, in some tables, sort assets into terciles of pre-sample β_SMB (high-β vs. low-β) and report average returns; however, the formal estimation uses the continuous βs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Linear K-factor structure  
   Excess return_i,t = α_i + β_i′F_t + ε_i,t .  Plausibility: standard in equilibrium models; widely validated.

A2. Factors are exogenous to asset-specific shocks  
   Cov(ε_i,t , F_t)=0. Plausible because factors are aggregate, tradable portfolios (Mkt-RF, SMB, HML) constructed without using asset-i’s return.

A3. Stationarity and ergodicity of returns and factors  
   Needed for consistent β estimates. Reasonable for monthly 1963–1991 data; we will test with KPSS/ADF.

A4. Cross-sectional variation in β  
   Required to identify λ in second pass. Stocks and bonds have very different loadings, so satisfied.

A5. No omitted priced factors (or, if omitted, PCA will detect)  
   We address by adding latent factors and performing Hansen–Jagannathan distance tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  

T1. Measurement error in β estimates (errors-in-variables bias in second pass)  
   • Use Shanken (1992) correction for β estimation error.  
   • Employ “full-sample iterated GMM” as robustness, which jointly estimates β and λ.

T2. Missing factors / model misspecification  
   • Run PCA on residuals; include additional factors (e.g., momentum, term-spread) if PCA suggests.  
   • Compare model pricing errors (GRS test) pre- and post-extension.

T3. Structural breaks (non-stationarity)  
   • Chow tests and rolling-window estimates (pre- and post-1979 Volcker shift).  
   • Allow time-varying λ_t using state-space/Kalman as robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE (executable)  

```r
#------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Packages
#------------------------------------------------
libs <- c("tidyverse","fixest","sandwich","lmtest","psych")  # PCA in psych
lapply(libs, require, character.only = TRUE)

#------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Data load
#   Assume RETURNS.csv has columns:
#   date, asset_id, excess_ret, mkt_rf, smb, hml, rf
#------------------------------------------------
ret  <- read_csv("RETURNS.csv") %>%
        mutate(date = as.Date(date))

#------------------------------------------------
# 2.  First-pass: estimate betas for each asset
#------------------------------------------------
first_pass <- feols(excess_ret ~ mkt_rf + smb + hml | asset_id,
                    data = ret, cluster = ~asset_id)

betas <- broom::tidy(first_pass) %>%      # extract coefficient table
         filter(term %in% c("mkt_rf","smb","hml")) %>%
         select(asset_id = fe, term, estimate) %>%
         pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate)

# merge betas back with average excess return per asset
avg_ret <- ret %>% group_by(asset_id) %>%
           summarise(mean_excess = mean(excess_ret, na.rm=TRUE))

cross_sec <- left_join(avg_ret, betas, by="asset_id") %>% drop_na()

#------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Second-pass: cross-sectional regression
#         E[ri] = λ0 + β_i*λ
#------------------------------------------------
sec_pass <- lm(mean_excess ~ mkt_rf + smb + hml, data = cross_sec)
coeftest(sec_pass, vcov.=vcovHC(sec_pass, type="HC3"))

# Shanken‐corrected standard errors
shanken_se <- function(sec, first){   # simple helper
  n       <- nrow(ret %>% distinct(date))
  factors <- ret %>% select(mkt_rf,smb,hml) %>% as.matrix()
  Sigma_f <- cov(factors)
  lam_hat <- coef(sec)[-1]
  V_beta  <- vcov(first)[c("mkt_rf","smb","hml"),
                          c("mkt_rf","smb","hml")]
  se_corr <- sqrt( diag( vcovHC(sec,"HC3")[-1,-1] +
              (1/n)*solve(Sigma_f) %*% V_beta %*% solve(Sigma_f) ) )
  return(se_corr)
}
shanken_se(sec_pass, first_pass)

#------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Robustness 1: PCA on asset returns
#------------------------------------------------
# wide asset x time matrix
R_wide <- ret %>% select(date, asset_id, excess_ret) %>%
          pivot_wider(names_from = asset_id, values_from = excess_ret) %>%
          select(-date) %>% as.matrix()
pca_out <- psych::principal(R_wide, nfactors = 3, rotate = "none")
print(pca_out$loadings)

# Correlate PCs with observed factors
factor_mat <- ret %>% select(mkt_rf,smb,hml)
cor_mat <- cor(factor_mat, pca_out$scores)
print(cor_mat)

#------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness 2: rolling βs (structural break)
#------------------------------------------------
library(zoo)
roll_fun <- function(x) coef(lm(excess_ret ~ mkt_rf + smb + hml, x))[-1]
roll_betas <- rollapply(ret, width = 120, by = 12, FUN = roll_fun,
                        by.column = FALSE, align = 'right')
plot.zoo(roll_betas)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Economic priors (monthly risk premia, 1963–1991):  
•  λ_MKT  ≈ 0.60 % (≈ 7 % annually) – equity premium.  
•  λ_SMB  ≈ 0.20 % (size premium).  
•  λ_HML  ≈ 0.30 % (value premium).  

Betas for government/AAA bonds should be near zero on SMB/HML and mildly positive on MKT, so predicted bond excess returns ≈ 0.1–0.2 %/month. We expect the three factors to explain a substantial share (adj-R² > 70 %) of cross-sectional variation versus a single-factor CAPM.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  

C1: Factor exogeneity (Cov(ε, F)=0)           1  
C2: Sufficient time observations for β         1  
C3: Cross-sectional variation in β             1  
C4: No important omitted priced factor         0 .5   (partly mitigated with PCA)  
C5: Stationarity / no structural breaks       0 .5   (tested with rolling estimates)

Total score: 4 / 5 .
